content.intro: This lesson covers Troubleshooting Incorrect Results as part of Formula Auditing, Security, and Troubleshooting. It follows the attached Excel curriculum, with an emphasis on small examples and verification.
content.why_it_matters: Troubleshooting Incorrect Results contributes to reliable business reporting and professional spreadsheet delivery. Document assumptions, verify results independently, and separate optional platform tools from core Excel behavior. Compatibility: Check Microsoft’s function reference for the target Excel version, platform, and update channel. Dynamic-array spill behavior and some newer functions are not available in every legacy installation.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Troubleshooting Incorrect Results focuses on the following parts of the supplied syllabus: Unexpected zeros; Incorrect range references; Data type mismatches; Hidden rows and filtered datasets. Keep the underlying source data visible and make each assumption explicit.

content_blocks.expected_output: Returns a readable fallback when the calculation raises an error; it does not distinguish every possible cause, so investigate unexpected errors rather than hiding them.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Test normal values, blank inputs and a zero denominator. Use Evaluate Formula and trace tools for complex workbooks; do not blanket-wrap every formula to conceal data problems.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Work in a duplicate workbook or a scratch sheet. Restore the input range and formula/code to the original state, clear filters or selections, then rerun the same test cases. Record expected and actual behavior rather than assuming a successful result.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a small, known dataset for troubleshooting incorrect results. Apply the example above, compute or inspect at least one result independently, then deliberately try a blank, duplicate, boundary, or not-found case where relevant.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small worksheet or workbook section that demonstrates troubleshooting incorrect results. Use clear headers, label units and assumptions, and capture expected versus actual output for a normal case and an edge case. Where the concept requires a specialized Excel feature, first verify that feature is available in your Excel edition.

content.task: Build or inspect an Excel example that demonstrates troubleshooting incorrect results; use the example to verify one normal and one edge case, and write down any version or tool dependency. For a complete curriculum practice scenario, also complete “Spreadsheet Audit” using the synthetic dataset `assets/data/practical-21-spreadsheet-audit.csv`; see the linked additional exercise file.
task_acceptance_criteria: The worksheet/workflow uses a clear, labeled source range and explicit assumptions.
The learner records an expected output and independently compares it with the actual result.
At least one relevant edge case is checked; data and formula errors are not silently concealed.
The workbook is saved as a copy and compatibility/security/accessibility notes are followed where relevant.
hints: Reduce the problem to a small range with known values before scaling it up.
Inspect cell values and formulas, not only displayed formatting; verify data types, references and range boundaries.
Compare expected versus actual results and check the Microsoft documentation for version-specific functions or tools.
content.expected_output: Returns a readable fallback when the calculation raises an error; it does not distinguish every possible cause, so investigate unexpected errors rather than hiding them.
common_mistakes: Assuming the displayed format is the same as the stored value or data type.
Using an incorrect range boundary, a mismatched lookup key, or an unverified assumption.
Trusting a result without comparing it with a known calculation or checking a failure/edge case.
summary: Troubleshooting Incorrect Results supports the workflow in Formula Auditing, Security, and Troubleshooting.
Use a small example, make assumptions visible, and verify the result against the source.
Check target-version availability and keep a clean copy before making high-impact changes.
